summary: A POC scoping call focused on private connectivity options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), region and egress constraints, and concrete success criteria for a 6-week pilot. Customer wants the inference plane isolated in their AWS account with control over egress and audit logs. Discussed workload sizing (concurrent sessions, avg tokens), benchmark plan, and timeline to validate latency + cost targets.
topics: Pilot success criteria (latency, throughput, SLOs, auditability)
Workload sizing: concurrent requests, typical sequence lengths
Benchmark plan and metrics to collect
Timeline and next steps for network dry-run and pilot kickoff
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll give a quick agenda then dive into network options and success criteria.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: Great thanks, we wanna make sure the inference traffic never leaves our control, so residency and egress policies are the top priority.
[00:20] Daniel Kim: Understood. We'll walk through two patterns folks use: VPC peering (direct network route into Redwood's service endpoints) and AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints where traffic terminates at an ENI in your VPC. Both have trade-offs on routing + egress.
[00:38] Tom Brooks: It needs to be in our account — we can't accept outbound calls to public internet for tokenization or anything.
[00:45] Maya Li: Right, so for a Private deployment pattern we can run Redwood Private inside your VPC or use PrivateLink to provide an endpoint that never traverses public internet. For your ask — is it a managed private plane or do you want Redwood running in your account?
[01:05] Lena Ortiz: Prefer Redwood-managed control plane but inference in our account. We want the runtime inside our VPC if possible — or at least endpoint that looks like it lives in our VPC.
[01:15] Daniel Kim: Okay that lines up with PrivateLink+dedicated-capacity model or Redwood Private on customer infra. PrivateLink keeps control in your account for egress but you still talk to Redwood-managed instances behind the endpoint.
[01:29] Arjun Mehta: Quick question — with PrivateLink, does egress to S3 or other aw s services go through our NAT? We need to ensure logs and artifacts stay in-region.
[01:40] Daniel Kim: Good call. Cache and model artifact pulls are done at provisioning time; for runtime egress (e.g., to your S3 bucket) we can configure the instance role to write to your bucket directly if the runtime is in your account. If we manage the instances, we can also configure VPC endpoints so traffic to S3 stays internal to region and under your routing. There is a subtle difference: with peering traffic is routed across the peering link; with PrivateLink you get endpoint IPs and AWS handles the pathing.
[02:10] Priya Rao: Security requirements: SOC2 plus we need KMS customer-managed keys for persistent storage and audit logs that show user+request ids. Also retention of logs for 1 year.
[02:23] Sofia Patel: We can support CMKs + audit log export. We'll share the SOC2 summary and the KMS integration notes after this call.
[02:31] Lena Ortiz: Success criteria for the pilot — if we define it now that helps. We're thinking: sustained 500 rps with 75th pct latency < 120ms token, and end-to-end 95th pct < 400ms for typical 40-token seqs. Also total cost per 1k tokens under a target.
[02:49] Daniel Kim: That's reasonable. For clarity, are you measuring token latency or request latency? We generally measure per-token throughput on the runtime and end-to-end includes network and request overhead.
[02:59] Lena Ortiz: End-to-end request latency is the product metric. Internal metric can be per-token.
[03:05] Sofia Patel: We'll define both in the benchmark. Proposed pilot success criteria in our template: throughput target (500 rps), 95th latency target (end-to-end), model output quality baseline (pass eval set), and security checklist completed.
[03:20] Arjun Mehta: Workload sizing: our current app does bursts up to 1.2k rps for short windows, but steady state for the feature will be 300-600 rps. Avg tokens per request about 35, peak sequence 256.
[03:35] Daniel Kim: That's helpful. For sizing we need concurrency, token distribution, and KV cache hit expectations. If you have prefix repetition, caching helps a lot.
[03:46] Tom Brooks: We do a lot of similar prompts — hope cache helps.
[03:50] Maya Li: We'll instrument a benchmark with a seeded prompt set — you shared benchmark-seed-prompts.csv earlier, yes?
[03:57] Lena Ortiz: Yep that's the file.
[04:02] Sofia Patel: For the pilot timeline — we recommend a 6-week pilot: week 0 network dry-run & provisioning, week 1 perf baseline, weeks 2-3 tuning and cost optimisation, weeks 4-5 production-like load tests, week 6 sign-off / rollback plan. Does that fit your timelines?
[04:19] Lena Ortiz: We want to go faster but security needs checks. 6 weeks OK if we can do parallel steps.
[04:25] Arjun Mehta: About peering vs PrivateLink: peering seems simpler in terms of IP routing but we worry about cross-account route propagation and central transit gateways. PrivateLink avoids route tables complexity but you get per-AZ ENIs and potential bottlenecks if not scaled. Any guidance on throughput per ENI?
[04:43] Daniel Kim: Good question. PrivateLink throughput generally follows ENI capacities; for production we provision N endpoints across AZs and Redwood's control plane does active routing. For your throughput we would recommend at least 3 endpoints across AZs and an autoscaling policy on the backend. We'll put numbers in the benchmark doc but expect PrivateLink to be fine for 500 rps with appropriate sizing.
[05:05] Priya Rao: What about egress controls — we want deny-by-default outbound and explicit NAT only for certain S3 buckets and KMS endpoints. Can Redwood operate in that posture?
[05:17] Daniel Kim: Yes. If we provision runtime in your account, instances can assume roles with no internet access and use VPC endpoints to reach S3/KMS which you control. If it's Redwood-managed but behind PrivateLink, we coordinate to ensure S3 writes use VPC endpoint interfaces or we write to your bucket via a presigned or cross-account role — we'll document options.
[05:39] Lena Ortiz: Auditability — we need request IDs and token-level accounting mapped to user IDs. Is that part of Redwood's telemetry?
[05:48] Maya Li: We emit per-request metadata (request id, model, prompts, response hashes) and can send logs to your S3 or CloudWatch via Kinesis/firehose. Token-level accounting is supported in the runtime; we can surface token counts in logs so you can reconcile billing/usage.
[06:05] Tom Brooks: Will those logs contain PII? We need to ensure logs can be masked or excluded.
[06:12] Daniel Kim: Yes, there is a redaction filter we can enable; you can also choose to store only hashes for prompt text. We'll add that to the security pack.
[06:21] Sofia Patel: Let's walk through a concrete baseline benchmark plan. Daniel?
[06:25] Daniel Kim: Sure. Step 1: baseline single-instance latency with 40-token seq and 1 concurrent request to validate model correctness. Step 2: scale to target concurrency to emulate 500 rps with realistic token distribution. We'll collect metrics: per-token time, GPU util, queue latency, and measured throughput. We'll also run canary with region-fenced traffic to verify egress paths.
[06:46] Arjun Mehta: For the benchmark run, what AWS account does Redwood use to run the load generator? We want traffic origin to be in our VPC to simulate real pathing.
[06:55] Daniel Kim: We can run load generators from an instance in your account (recommended) or from a Redwood test account. For network validation we'll run from your SRE hosts — that's the dry-run.
[07:05] Lena Ortiz: Good. On telemetry and SLOs, we want per-route dashboards and an SLA for 99.5% availability during pilot. Is that negotiable?
[07:15] Sofia Patel: For pilots we typically commit to operational targets and provide dashboard access. Formal SLA is part of Dedicated/Private contracts, but we'll offer reliability commitments during the pilot and share our runbooks.
[07:28] Priya Rao: One more item — regions and data residency. All data must remain in us-east-1. No cross-region fallback unless explicitly permitted.
[07:36] Daniel Kim: We can pin instances to a region and disable cross-region failover for the pilot. We'll document the fallback policy for production but keep it disabled for this POC.
[07:45] Lena Ortiz: Cost guardrails — we need a cost cap during pilot and alerts at 60% and 85%.
[07:51] Maya Li: We'll set usage quotas and alert hooks with webhook notifications to your finance and infra channels.
[07:58] Tom Brooks: On the PrivateLink vs peering decision — leaning PrivateLink for isolation and simpler route tables, but concerned about AZ capacity. If we do PrivateLink, how do you handle cross-AZ traffic and balancing?
[08:10] Daniel Kim: Redwood will provision endpoints across AZs, use sticky routing to avoid cross-AZ hairpin, and can scale backends per AZ. We'll include a diagram in the checklist showing endpoint to AZ mapping.
[08:23] Sofia Patel: Action recap: Redwood to share security pack, PrivateLink checklist, and initial benchmark plan. Nimbus to share VPC CIDRs and required KMS policies. We'll schedule the network dry-run.
[08:35] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. A couple small clarifications — do you support customer-managed HSM for keys?
[08:43] Daniel Kim: We support CMKs. For customer HSM we need a short architecture review; it's possible if keys are available in the same region. We'll add that as a follow-up.
[08:54] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[09:00] Sofia Patel: Thanks — last thing: we'll include measurable success criteria in the pilot POC doc: throughput, 95th and 99th latency targets, quality pass rate on eval prompts, security checklist complete, and log retention verified.
[09:14] Lena Ortiz: Ok team, please send the checklist and we'll aim to sign off on the network dry-run next Wednesday if possible.
[09:23] Daniel Kim: We'll get that out by Friday.
[09:28] Priya Rao: Thanks all.
[09:30] Sofia Patel: Thanks everyone. End call.

Notes: occasional transcription mismatches observed (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache", "privatelink" sometimes lowercased); speaker attribution occasionally generic. Benchmark sheet link: https://crm.example.com/benchmark-seed-prompts.csv
